sections.h: Tacitus's five origins and his Egyptian story
sections.b: In Histories 5:2 Tacitus lists five origins of the Jews: refugees from Crete (the name Judaei from Mount Ida); Egyptians led by Hierosolymus and Judas; Ethiopians; Assyrian newcomers who took part of Egypt; and Homer's Solymi. At 5:3 he gives the story "most writers agree" on: a disease in Egypt, an oracle of Hammon, and an exile led by Moyses. Josephus names Manetho, Cheremon and Lysimachus as the Egyptian tellers of that tale and answers them (Against Apion 1.14-35). Strabo, a Greek geographer, tells instead of Moses as an Egyptian priest who left because he rejected Egypt's animal images (Geography 16.2.35). Bloch's study (reviewed by van der Horst) sets Tacitus's passage in the Greek and Roman ethnographic pattern of origin, customs, land and history.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Genesis 29:35; Exodus 3:10; Numbers 12:1

claude.title: Where the stories touch Genesis
claude.body: My reading: the five stories are not random. The "Assyrian" story gives the outline of Genesis (from the east, through Egypt, to the Hebrew country); "Judas" gives Judah's name; the Ethiopian story may echo Moses' Cushite wife; and "Solymi" is close to the city's old name Salem. Each is garbled, but the Bible's shape shows through.
claude.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Genesis 11:31; Genesis 14:18; Genesis 29:35; Numbers 12:1

sections.b: Tacitus's Moyses (5:3-4) is an exile in a plague camp who tells the crowd to trust themselves, finds water by following wild asses, and then gives new rites "the opposite of what everyone else does." In Exodus the LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh (Exodus 3:10), the water comes at God's word (Exodus 17:6), and the law comes at Sinai (Exodus 20). Josephus reports Manetho's version in which an Egyptian priest, Osarsiph, "or Moses," makes laws opposite to Egypt's (Against Apion 1.26) and answers that Egyptians themselves called Moses "a wonderful and a divine person" (1.31). Strabo, in a friendlier report, makes Moses a priest who taught that God has no image (Geography 16.2.35). Stephen says that "Moses was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22), which is the grain of truth behind the Egyptian-Moses stories.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Exodus 3:10; Exodus 17:6; Exodus 20:1-17; Acts 7:22

sections.h: Unleavened bread in Tacitus and the coup at the feast
sections.b: Tacitus says Jewish unleavened bread is kept "as proof of the grain they grabbed in a hurry" (5:4). Exodus: "the people picked up their dough before it rose" (Exodus 12:34), and Deuteronomy calls it "the bread of hardship, because you came out of the land of Egypt in a rush" (Deuteronomy 16:3). Josephus names the feast on which John seized the temple: "the feast of unleavened bread ... when it is believed the Jews were first freed from the Egyptians" (Jewish War 5.3.1), and says the Romans caught crowds who had "come up from all the country to the feast of unleavened bread" (6.9.3).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Exodus 12:34; Exodus 12:39; Deuteronomy 16:3

sections.h: The Sabbath as laziness, and the planet Saturn
sections.b: Tacitus gives the Sabbath two explanations: the Jews rested on the seventh day because it ended their labors, "charmed by idleness" they also gave the seventh year to laziness (5:4); or the day honors Saturn (5:4). The Bible gives creation and the Exodus as the reasons (Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 5:15) and says the rest is for people and animals alike (Deuteronomy 5:14; Mark 2:27). Josephus quotes the writer Apion, who said the word Sabbath came from a disease of the groin, and calls it a trifle (Against Apion 2.2). Christians divide on how the day binds today (see the card on Histories 5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15; Mark 2:27

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews, charmed by idleness, "gave the seventh year to laziness too" (5:4). Leviticus gives the reason: "the land is to have a Sabbath of complete rest" (Leviticus 25:4), and Exodus adds that "the needy of your people can eat from it" (Exodus 23:11). A Roman reader saw only a year without work; the Law has a year of rest for the land and food for the poor.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 25:1-7; Exodus 23:10-11

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews "set up circumcision so that they'd be recognized by the difference," and that converts take up the same practice (5:5). Genesis calls it "the sign of the covenant" (Genesis 17:11), given to Abraham, not invented by Moyses. Josephus answers a Greek critic by noting Egypt's priests were circumcised too (Against Apion 2.14). The New Testament debates whether Gentile believers must be circumcised (Acts 15:1; Acts 16:3; Romans 2:25-29). Jeremiah lists Egypt with Judah, Edom, Ammon and Moab among the peoples "circumcised in a foreskin" (Jeremiah 9:25-26).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Genesis 17:9-14; Acts 15:1; Acts 16:3; Romans 2:25-29; Jeremiah 9:25-26

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews avoid pork "in memory of the disaster" of a skin disease that pigs are prone to (5:4). Leviticus gives a plainer reason: the pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud, so "It is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7). Josephus replies that Egypt's own priests abstain from swine's flesh (Against Apion 2.14). In the New Testament Peter's vision (Acts 10:15) and Mark's comment that Jesus "made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19) change what the food laws mean for Gentile and Jewish believers. Pigs mark a later fight over the Law too: Antiochus's decree was "to sacrifice pigs and unclean animals" (1 Maccabees 1:47).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 11:7-8; Deuteronomy 14:8; Acts 10:13-15; Mark 7:18-19; 1 Maccabees 1:47

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews "admit their long-ago hunger by frequent fasts" (5:4). The Law's yearly fast is on the Day of Atonement: "you are to humble yourselves and do no work at all" (Leviticus 16:29). Zechariah names four fasts in the year, in the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months (Zechariah 8:19). In a parable a Pharisee boasts, "Twice a week I fast" (Luke 18:12). Josephus says the high priest wore plain clothes into the holy place on the one day a year "that day when our custom is for all of us to keep a fast to God" (Jewish War 5.5.7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 16:29-31; Zechariah 8:19; Luke 18:12

sections.h: No statues in Jewish worship, as Rome saw it
sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews "understand only with the mind, and one divine power"; they call profane those who make images of God "in human form out of perishable materials," and they put up "no statues in their cities, let alone in their temples" (5:5). Exodus 20:4 and Deuteronomy 4:15-19 are the Law behind it, and Paul at Athens uses the same argument: "we should not suppose that the Divine looks like gold or silver or stone" (Acts 17:29). Strabo reports Moses teaching that no one should fabricate an image of God resembling any creature (Geography 16.2.35). Christians differ on images in worship and on honoring them (see the card on Histories 5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Exodus 20:4-5; Deuteronomy 4:15-19; Acts 17:29

sections.h: One divine power, known by the mind
sections.b: Tacitus's summary of Jewish belief is accurate: the Jews "understand only with the mind, and one divine power," and hold that "the supreme and eternal being can't be copied and will never die" (5:5). It is the creed of Deuteronomy 6:4, "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one." Even a hostile Roman states it correctly. The same chapter has him say the Jews "despise the gods" of others, which he counts a fault and the Bible counts a duty (Exodus 20:3).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 20:3

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews pay neither kings nor Caesars the flattery of statues (5:5). The dispute over Caligula's statue in the temple, which Tacitus mentions at 5:9, was the sharpest case; Josephus tells how crowds met Petronius at Ptolemais and pleaded for their laws (Jewish War 2.10). In the Gospels Jesus separates Caesar's coin from God's claim (Mark 12:17), and the charge against Christians in Thessalonica is that they say Jesus is "another king" (Acts 17:7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Mark 12:13-17; Acts 17:7; John 19:15

sections.b: In Histories 5:5, 5:8 and 5:13 Tacitus calls the Jews' other customs "twisted and foul," their way "absurd and sordid," the nation "the vilest" and prone to "superstition." He says they feel "hostile hatred" toward everyone else, though loyal and pitying among themselves. Bloch's study of the passage, as van der Horst reviews it, argues that even neutral features "receive a non-positive colouring" and that the passage aims to show that the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and lose their only temple. Bloch also says this does not make Tacitus the "notorious Jew-hater" he is often said to be. Van der Horst's review traces how the passage was received: Tertullian calls Tacitus a liar; the first commentators, in the 16th and 17th centuries, "usually react rather mildly"; Jewish commentators of the 17th century answered it; Voltaire and Gibbon sympathized with its anti-Jewish views in the 18th century, and it was put to anti-Jewish use in the 19th century and in the Nazi period. A Christian reader weighs each charge against the Law and the New Testament and does not repeat the insults as fact.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Esther 3:8

sections.b: Tacitus says converts "take up the same practice," and that the worst men of other nations sent tribute and gifts to the temple (5:5). The New Testament knows converts (Matthew 23:15), a court official who "had come to Jerusalem to worship" (Acts 8:27), the God-fearing centurion Cornelius (Acts 10:2), and the rule that kept Jews from visiting foreigners (Acts 10:28). Tacitus's "they keep away from foreign women" matches Deuteronomy 7:3 and Ezra 9:1-2.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Matthew 23:15; Acts 8:27-28; Acts 10:1-2; Acts 10:28; Deuteronomy 7:3-4; Ezra 9:1-2

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews "eat separately and sleep separately" (5:5). Acts 10:28 and Galatians 2:12 show Jewish believers holding back from table fellowship with Gentiles, and Paul opposing it. Ephesians 2:14 says Christ "broke down the middle wall."
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Acts 10:28; Galatians 2:11-14; Ephesians 2:14

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews bury their dead, "following the Egyptian custom," with the same care and belief about the underworld (5:5). The Bible's burials begin with Sarah's cave (Genesis 23:19-20); Jacob and Joseph were embalmed in Egypt (Genesis 50:2-3, 50:26); Saul's body was burned and his bones buried (1 Samuel 31:12-13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Genesis 23:19-20; Genesis 50:2-3; 1 Samuel 31:12-13

sections.h: Eternal souls, as Tacitus describes them
sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews think "the souls of those killed in battle or by execution are eternal" (5:5). Josephus has his own speech at Jotapata say "the soul is ever immortal" (Jewish War 3.8.5) and says the Essenes teach immortal souls (2.8.11). Daniel promises that "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up" (Daniel 12:2). Acts says the Pharisees affirm the resurrection and the Sadducees deny it (Acts 23:8).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Daniel 12:2; Acts 23:8; Matthew 22:23

sections.h: The gods of the nations in Book 5
sections.b: Tacitus says converts learn first "to despise the gods" (5:5); the omens at the temple include a voice that "the gods were leaving" (5:13); and Civilis calls on "the gods of Germany" (5:17). The Bible has the nations sacrificing "to demons, not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20). Christians read this in different ways: as empty idols or as real powers behind them. This site's topic on the divine council covers the second reading.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Histories of Tacitus 5:17; Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20

sections.b: Tacitus says that because the priests used flutes and drums and were wreathed in ivy, and "a golden vine was found in the temple," some decided the Jews worshiped Liber (5:5). He rejects the idea. The golden vine was real. Josephus describes golden vines above the gate of the temple building, with clusters "as tall as a man's height" (Jewish War 5.5.4), a golden vine over the doors of Herod's temple (Antiquities 15.11.3), and a golden vine that Aristobulus sent to Pompey (Antiquities 14.3.1). The Bible's own vine is Israel: "A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved" (Psalm 80:8), the vineyard of Isaiah 5:1-7, and Jesus' "I am the real vine" (John 15:1). The passages quoted from Josephus do not say what the temple's vine stood for; that it recalled Israel is a reading, not a statement of theirs.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; John 15:1

sections.h: The temple as Tacitus and Josephus describe it
sections.b: Tacitus describes a temple of "immense wealth," shut away in the innermost part, with only priests at the threshold (5:8), built like a citadel with colonnades, a spring and cisterns (5:12), and burned by John's men with the grain (5:12). Josephus describes the same courts and the Antonia fortress at its corner (Jewish War 5.5). The Gospels have Jesus say "not one stone will be left on a stone" (Mark 13:2), and Acts has a mob accusing Paul of bringing Greeks in (Acts 21:28). At 5:9 Tacitus says Pompey found an empty seat and no image; Josephus says Pompey saw the lampstand, table and gold vessels (Jewish War 1.7.6) in the outer sanctuary, and that the inmost room held "nothing at all" (5.5.5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Mark 13:1-2; Acts 21:28-29; John 2:20

sections.b: Tacitus's omens before the siege (5:13) include a temple lit by fire from the clouds and shrine doors that swung open. Josephus puts the light, the gate and the voice "Let us remove hence" at the feasts before the war (Jewish War 6.5.3). Ezekiel's vision had the LORD's glory leave the first temple before it fell (Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:23).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Matthew 23:38

sections.b: Tacitus calls Jerusalem the nation's capital and its site "high" and strong, on two hills with sloping walls, towers sixty and 120 feet high, the Antonia tower, a temple like a citadel and a spring that never ran dry (5:8, 5:11-12). He tells the city's history from Pompey to the war and the three commanders inside (5:9-12). Jesus wept over it and foretold that enemies would "ring you round" (Luke 19:41-44). Josephus gives the full siege (Jewish War 5-6); Tacitus's own account is lost where the text breaks off.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Histories of Tacitus 5:11; Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 23:37-38

sections.b: Tacitus's "two hills of enormous height" (5:11) are the pair Josephus describes: the upper city on the higher hill, which David called the Citadel, and the lower city (Jewish War 5.4.1). Psalm 76:2 has God's "den in Zion."
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:11; Psalm 76:2

sections.h: The Tenth Legion on the Mount of Olives
sections.b: Josephus puts the 10th legion on the Mount of Olives during the siege (Jewish War 5.3.5). It is the hill where Jesus sat for his talk on the temple's fall (Matthew 24:3). Tacitus names the 10th among the legions Titus gathered (5:1) but does not mention the hill.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Matthew 24:3

sections.b: Titus takes the field with the 5th, 10th and 15th legions, the 12th and detachments from Alexandria (5:1); Tacitus summarizes Rome and Judea from Pompey to the war under Florus and Cestius Gallus and Nero's choice of Vespasian (5:9-10); the Romans fight at the walls (5:11); three commanders hold the city, and John seizes the temple under cover of a sacrifice (5:12); omens and an oracle that the crowd read as their own (5:13). Josephus gives the same events at greater length: the army (Jewish War 5.1.6), the factions (5.1), John's attack at the feast of unleavened bread (5.3.1), the omens (6.5.3), the oracle (6.5.4) and the dead (6.9.3). Luke 19:41-44 and Luke 21:20-24 give Jesus' warnings of the same siege. The text of the Histories breaks off before the city falls.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:10; Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 24:1-2

claude.title: Two Roman voices on one war
claude.body: My reading: set Tacitus 5:1-13 beside Luke 21 and Josephus 5-6 and you get three witnesses of different kinds: a prophecy before the war (Luke), a Jewish eyewitness during it (Josephus), and a Roman historian a generation later (Tacitus). They overlap on the army, the factions, the omens and the oracle, which is why a Christian reader can use all three together.

sections.b: Jesus told his disciples that "not one stone will be left on a stone" (Matthew 24:2) and "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). Tacitus 5:1 has Titus encamp "not far from Jerusalem" and 5:13 has earthworks; Josephus has the Romans ring the city with a wall (Jewish War 5.12). Many Christians read Luke 21:20-24 as fulfilled in AD 70, some also see a further fulfillment still ahead; this site shows both on the topic.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Matthew 24:1-2; Luke 19:43-44; Luke 21:20-24

sections.b: Tacitus lists "armies ... clashing across the sky, weapons glowing red" among the omens (5:13). Josephus has "chariots and troops of soldiers in their armor ... running about among the clouds" (Jewish War 6.5.3). Jesus spoke of "terrors, and great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11) and "signs in the sun, the moon and the stars" (Luke 21:25).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Luke 21:11; Luke 21:25

sections.h: Omens at the temple, and why the crowd did not atone
sections.b: In 5:13 Tacitus says the Jews were "prone to superstition but hostile to religious rites" and would not make up for the omens "with sacrifices or vows," the Roman remedy (hostiae and vota). A Roman expected to atone for a prodigy with sacrifice; the Jews read their omens by their own writings. Josephus says "the men of learning" read them as warnings while the common people took the opened gate as lucky (Jewish War 6.5.3).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13

sections.b: Tacitus says most of the besieged were convinced their priests' ancient writings said "men setting out from Judea would rule the world," and that the riddles predicted Vespasian and Titus (5:13). Josephus calls it "an ambiguous oracle" found in their sacred writings and applies it to Vespasian (Jewish War 6.5.4); Suetonius reports "a firm persuasion" through the East of an empire to devolve on some who should go forth from Judaea (Vespasian 4). The Bible's candidate texts include Numbers 24:17, Genesis 49:10 and Daniel 7:13-14. Christians read the promised ruler as Jesus (Matthew 2:2; Luke 1:32-33) and warn against the rebel messiahs (Matthew 24:23-24).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Numbers 24:17; Genesis 49:10; Daniel 7:13-14; Matthew 2:1-2; Luke 1:32-33; Matthew 24:23-24

claude.title: A promise claimed by the winner
claude.body: My reading: three Roman-age writers give the same oracle to the Flavians. That is how an ambiguous promise can be claimed by the winner. The Christian claim is that the promise belongs to the one the Gospels name, whose kingdom "will have no end" (Luke 1:33).

sections.h: False prophets and omens in the siege; women prophets
sections.b: Josephus says false prophets urged people to the temple and "a great number of false prophets suborned by the tyrants" kept hope alive in the siege (Jewish War 6.5.2), as Jesus warned: "false messiahs and false prophets will rise up" (Matthew 24:24). At 5:22 Tacitus's German seer Veleda is given a captured ship as a gift; the Bible has Deborah (Judges 4:4) and Huldah (2 Kings 22:14) who spoke for the LORD.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Histories of Tacitus 5:22; Matthew 24:24; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14

sections.h: Sodom and the plain, in Tacitus and Josephus
sections.b: Tacitus reports that plains near the lake "were once rich and home to great cities, until lightning struck and burned them," and the ground has stayed barren; he adds his own view that the lake's fumes poisoned it (5:7). Josephus says the country of Sodom "was burnt by lightning" and that traces of the five cities remain (Jewish War 4.8.4); Strabo reports local belief in thirteen cities with Sodom as chief (Geography 16.2.44). Genesis: "the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD, out of the sky" (Genesis 19:24). Moses also describes such a land: "burned out with sulfur and salt, unsown, growing nothing" (Deuteronomy 29:23), and the Wisdom of Solomon, a book some churches hold as Scripture, has "a barren land that sends up smoke" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:7; Genesis 13:10; Genesis 19:24-28; Deuteronomy 29:23; Wisdom of Solomon 10:7

claude.title: A Roman who kept the story
claude.body: My reading: Tacitus is the clearest case in his book where an outsider keeps the Bible's story almost whole, rich plain, many cities, fire from the sky, a land that stays dead. He changes the cause (fumes) but not the event.

sections.h: The lake in Tacitus, Josephus and the Bible
sections.b: Tacitus describes the lake at the end of the Jordan: huge, like a sea, foul-tasting, with deadly air for those who live near, no fish, water that holds up swimmers and non-swimmers alike, and bitumen it throws up at one season (5:6). Josephus says the same: the water bears up the heaviest things, Vespasian had bound men thrown in and they floated, and black clods of bitumen are hauled into ships (Jewish War 4.8.4). Genesis calls it the Salt Sea and the Valley of Siddim "full of tar pits" (Genesis 14:3, 14:10); Ezekiel sees it healed (Ezekiel 47:8-9).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:6; Genesis 14:3; Genesis 14:10; Joshua 3:16; Ezekiel 47:8-9

sections.b: Tacitus says Lebanon "feeds the river Jordan and sends it on its way," and the river flows "through one lake and another and is held in the third" (5:6). Joshua has the river stand still to let Israel cross to the Salt Sea side: "The water flowing down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, was cut off completely" (Joshua 3:16).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:6; Joshua 3:15-17; Deuteronomy 3:25

sections.b: Tacitus describes the balsam tree of Judea, whose sap is opened with a chip of stone or a piece of pottery because iron makes the veins shrink, and says doctors use the sap (5:6). Josephus names the balsam of Jericho "the most precious of all the fruits" there (Jewish War 4.8.3). Ishmaelite traders carried "gum, balm and myrrh" to Egypt (Genesis 37:25), and Jeremiah asks, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:6; Genesis 37:25; Jeremiah 8:22; Judges 1:16

sections.b: Tacitus says some link the Jewish seventh day to Saturn, whose star has the highest orbit and greatest power among seven that rule human lives (5:4). The Bible does not rest the Sabbath on the stars. It forbids bowing to them: "do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). Isaiah mocks the advisers "who stare at the stars" (Isaiah 47:13). Cassius Dio says the custom of naming the days after the seven planets came from the Egyptians (Roman History 37.18).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 47:13; Jeremiah 10:2

sections.h: Egypt in Tacitus's account of the Jews
sections.b: Tacitus makes Egypt the source of the Jews on three of his stories: the crowd under Isis, the Assyrians who took part of Egypt, and the plague that Bocchoris cast out (5:2-3), and says Jewish burial and dislike of animal worship come from or against Egypt (5:4-5). In Genesis, Egypt is a refuge in famine (Genesis 12:10) and the house of slavery in Exodus (Exodus 12:33-39). Josephus calls the Egyptians "the first that cast reproaches upon us" (Against Apion 1.25).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Genesis 12:10; Exodus 12:33-39

sections.b: Tacitus lists a Jewish origin from Ethiopians driven out by fear and hatred of their neighbors under King Cepheus (5:2). Ethiopia is the Bible's Cush. Moses took a Cushite wife (Numbers 12:1), and Josephus tells of his Ethiopian campaign and marriage to Tharbis (Antiquities 2.10.2).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Numbers 12:1

sections.b: Tacitus's fourth origin is that the Jews were Assyrian settlers, short of land, who took part of Egypt and moved on to the Hebrew country (5:2). Genesis has Abram's family leave Ur of the Chaldeans for Haran and Canaan (Genesis 11:31); Josephus's retelling of the war on Sodom (Genesis 14) says that the Assyrians then had dominion over Asia and made war on the Sodomites (Antiquities 1.9.1, in Whiston's English).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Genesis 11:31; Genesis 14:13

sections.b: Tacitus's first origin is that the Jews were refugees from Crete, and he derives "Judaei" from the Idaei of Mount Ida (5:2). The Bible's name comes from Judah (Genesis 29:35). Crete in the Bible is another matter: see this topic.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Genesis 29:35

sections.h: Persians and the Jews in Tacitus
sections.b: Tacitus says that while the East belonged to the Assyrians, Medes and Persians the Jews were the most despised of subject peoples (5:8). In the Bible, Persia is where Cyrus lets the exiles go (Ezra 1:1-4) and where Haman says of them, "Their laws are unlike any other people's" (Esther 3:8).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Ezra 1:1-4; Esther 3:8

sections.b: Tacitus, naming only a king Antiochus, says he "tried to strip away their superstition and give them Greek ways" but was stopped by the Parthian war (5:8). 1 Maccabees tells the same attempt as persecution: "each was to give up his own customs" and "they built an abomination of desolation on the altar" (1 Maccabees 1:42, 1:54), and has the king go east for money (1 Maccabees 3:31; 1 Maccabees 6:1-4). Josephus says he took the temple's gold for want of money (Against Apion 2.7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:8; 1 Maccabees 1:41-43; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 3:31; 1 Maccabees 6:1-4; Daniel 11:31

sections.b: Tacitus says that after the Macedonians weakened the Jews "set up kings for themselves," who were driven out by the fickle crowd, won back power by arms, and killed brothers, wives and parents, using the priesthood as the base of their power (5:8). Josephus says Aristobulus, the first to wear the crown, was cruel to his mother and brothers (Antiquities 13.11) and Alexander Jannaeus was pelted with citrons at the festival (Antiquities 13.13.5).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Genesis 49:10

sections.h: Herod, Simon, the three rulers and Agrippa in Tacitus
sections.b: Tacitus tells in one paragraph how Rome's Herod and his sons fit the story: Antony gave Herod the kingdom and Augustus enlarged it; after his death a man named Simon seized the royal title (Josephus: a servant of the king, killed by Gratus, Jewish War 2.4.2); the nation was ruled in three parts by Herod's children (5:9). Matthew's Herod and Archelaus (Matthew 2:1; Matthew 2:22) and Luke's tetrarchs (Luke 3:1) are those men. At 5:1 Agrippa is a king in Titus's army; he is the King Agrippa of Acts 25-26.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Matthew 2:1; Matthew 2:22; Luke 3:1; Acts 25:13; Acts 26:2-3

sections.b: Acts has Agrippa and Bernice at Caesarea hearing Paul (Acts 25:13, 25:23). Tacitus 5:1 names only the king Agrippa. Josephus says Bernice was Agrippa's sister, widowed by Herod of Chalcis, rumored to be too close to her brother, and briefly married to Polemo of Cilicia (Antiquities 20.7.3). Suetonius tells of Titus's "well-known attachment to queen Berenice", who "received from him, as it is reported, a promise of marriage", and says that when Titus became emperor he "immediately sent away Berenice from the city" (Titus 7). An editor's note in that Thomson-Forester translation adds that she lived in Rome with Titus.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Acts 25:13; Acts 25:23

sections.h: Rome and Judea from Pompey to Felix
sections.b: Tacitus gives one paragraph of Roman history in Judea: Pompey the first Roman to conquer the Jews; Pacorus and the Parthians; Ventidius and Sosius; Herod; Simon; Varus; the three sons; quiet under Tiberius; Caligula's statue; Claudius handing the province to Knights or freedmen, one of them Felix (5:9). The New Testament world is this world: Luke's Augustus and Tiberius (Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1), Acts' famine and expulsion under Claudius (Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2) and its governors Felix and Festus (Acts 24:27).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2; Acts 24:27

sections.b: Tacitus passes over the years of Pilate and Jesus in three words, sub Tiberio quies (5:9). In the Annals he writes that Christus "suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus" (Annals 15.44, Church and Brodribb). Luke dates John's start by Tiberius's fifteenth year and Pilate's governorship (Luke 3:1).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Luke 3:1; Luke 23:1-2

sections.b: Tacitus says Nero sent Vespasian after Cestius Gallus died (5:10). Suetonius says Vespasian was chosen for his skill and his obscure origin, and that astrologers told Nero he would have the rule of the East and some said "the kingdom of Jerusalem" (Vespasian 4; Nero 40). Paul's appeal "to Caesar" was to Nero (Acts 25:11).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:10; Acts 25:11; Acts 28:30-31

sections.b: Tacitus says the factions burned "a great store of grain" (5:12). Josephus says almost all the corn that would have lasted for a siege of many years was burned, and adds that the famine took the city (Jewish War 5.1.4). Luke 21:11 lists famines among the signs.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Luke 21:11

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews put the statue of the animal that guided them to water in the inner shrine (5:4). The Bible's best-known animal image in Israel's worship is Aaron's calf, which Moses judged a sin (Exodus 32:4). King Jeroboam later made two golden calves for Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-29), and King Hezekiah crushed the bronze snake Moses had made, because Israel had been burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). The cherubim over the ark were commanded sculptures (Exodus 25:18-20). Josephus answers the slander that an ass's head of gold stood in the temple (Against Apion 2.7).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Exodus 32:1-6; Exodus 20:4; 1 Kings 12:28-29; 2 Kings 18:4; Exodus 25:18-20

sections.b: Tacitus says the Jews sacrifice a ram "as if to insult Hammon" and an ox because the Egyptians worship Apis (5:4). The Law commands the offerings (Leviticus 1:1-9) and the first Passover carries this judgment: "on all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments" (Exodus 12:12). Josephus answers the writer Apion that Greeks and Macedonians offer whole hecatombs (Against Apion 2.14). The nearest Bible parallels show Egypt's own dislike of Israel's sacrifices and herds: "What we sacrifice to the LORD our God is a thing the Egyptians abhor" (Exodus 8:26) and "Egyptians loathe every shepherd" (Genesis 46:34).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 1:1-9; Exodus 12:12; Exodus 8:26; Genesis 46:34

sections.h: Laws "the opposite of what everyone else does"
sections.b: Tacitus says Moyses gave rites opposite to other peoples (5:4). Josephus says Manetho's Osarsiph made laws "mainly opposite to the customs of the Egyptians" (Against Apion 1.26). The Law says Israel is to be set apart: "be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44) and "a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 11:44-45; Exodus 19:5-6

sections.h: "They drove out the people living there"
sections.b: Tacitus compresses the conquest to one sentence: after six days of travel, on the seventh they "drove out the people living there and took the land" (5:3). The Bible has forty years in the wilderness, the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 3:17) and a land promised to Abraham.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Joshua 3:15-17

sections.h: A disease that turns the plagues around
sections.b: Tacitus has a disease in Egypt that disfigured bodies and an oracle ordering the sick people expelled (5:3). Exodus has plagues fall on Egypt and the king urge the Israelites out (Exodus 12:31-33). Josephus reports Lysimachus and Manetho calling the Jews "leprous and scabby" and answers that they could not have been so many (Against Apion 1.34-35).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Exodus 12:31-33

sections.b: Tacitus explains the pork ban by a skin disease that the Jews once had and pigs are prone to (5:4); the expelled crowd in his 5:3 is likewise diseased. Leviticus treats a skin disease (tsara'at) as a matter of purity, not as the reason for Israel's food laws. See the topic on skin disease.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Histories of Tacitus 5:4; Leviticus 11:7

sections.h: Felix in Tacitus, Acts, Josephus and Suetonius
sections.b: Tacitus (5:9): Antonius Felix, using "every kind of cruelty and lust," exercised a king's power with a slave's mind; he married Drusilla, Cleopatra and Antony's granddaughter. In the Annals he is the brother of Pallas, whom Tacitus calls a freedman (Annals 12.53), and held Samaria while Cumanus held Galilee (Annals 12.54). Josephus: Claudius sent "Felix, the brother of Pallas" (Antiquities 20.7.1); he fell in love with Drusilla, Agrippa II's sister, and won her away from Azizus of Emesa (20.7.2). Suetonius: lists him among Claudius's freedmen; Claudius made him governor of Judea and he became "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28). Acts: he is "the governor" (Acts 23:24), listens to Paul with Drusilla, "his own wife, a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24), grows afraid when Paul speaks of judgment, hopes for a bribe and leaves Paul in chains after two years (Acts 24:25-27). Same man: very likely. Drusilla: most likely two wives of the same name.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Acts 23:24-26; Acts 24:1-27; Acts 25:14

claude.title: A governor who feared the message
claude.body: My reading: Tacitus gives the verdict of the Roman record, Acts gives the scene in the room. Tacitus's cruelty and lust and Acts' greed and fear are two angles on one corrupt official. Paul's choice of topics, "righteousness, ... self-control and ... the judgment that lies ahead" (Acts 24:25), is aimed at the man Tacitus describes.

sections.h: Pilate, Felix, Florus and Cestius in Histories 5:9-10
sections.b: Tacitus names procurators and a legate in the story of Judea: Felix (5:9), Gessius Florus, under whom the war broke out, and Cestius Gallus, the legate of Syria whose attempt to put down the revolt went badly (5:10). Felix and his successor Festus are the governors of Acts 23-26. Pilate, though not named in the Histories, is "one of our procurators" in the Annals (15.44). Josephus gives Florus a chapter of his own (Jewish War 2.14).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Histories of Tacitus 5:10; Acts 23:24; Acts 24:27; Luke 3:1

sections.b: Tacitus says Claudius gave the province of Judea to "Roman Knights or freedmen" (5:9), and he names Felix as one of them. The New Testament's governor Felix (Acts 23:24) was, in Josephus's words, the brother of Pallas (Antiquities 20.7.1), and Suetonius lists Felix among Claudius's freedmen (Claudius 28).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Acts 23:24

sections.b: Tacitus describes Judea's borders, rare rain and rich soil, its balsam and palms, its villages and towns, and Jerusalem as the capital (5:6, 5:8). Matthew places Jesus' birth in Judea and Luke Pilate's rule there (Matthew 2:1; Luke 3:1). Josephus says Titus's legions came to Jerusalem by Emmaus and Jericho (Jewish War 5.1.6).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:6; Histories of Tacitus 5:8; Matthew 2:1; Luke 3:1

sections.h: Titus at the head of the army
sections.b: Tacitus says Titus was chosen by his father to finish the conquest of Judea and tells how he gathered the army and camped near Jerusalem (5:1). Josephus says he marched out of Caesarea with the three legions that had been with Vespasian and the 12th (Jewish War 5.1.6) and later fixed the camp near the city.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:11

sections.b: Tacitus says the riddles about a ruler from Judea "had really predicted Vespasian and Titus" (5:13). Josephus says the oracle "certainly denoted the government of Vespasian" (Jewish War 6.5.4), and Suetonius reports that the belief "referred to a Roman emperor, as the event shewed" (Vespasian 4).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:13; Numbers 24:17; Daniel 7:13-14

sections.b: Josephus is the main surviving witness for the siege Tacitus's text promises and does not reach. He names the legions (Jewish War 5.1.6), the three leaders (5.1), the feast on which John seized the temple (5.3.1), the omens (6.5.3) and the oracle (6.5.4), and answers the Egyptian stories Tacitus repeats (Against Apion 1-2). Where the two differ (Bargioras, Varus or Gratus, Drusilla), this site's notes weigh them.
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1; Histories of Tacitus 5:3; Histories of Tacitus 5:12; Histories of Tacitus 5:13

sections.h: Tacitus as a writer on the Jews
sections.b: Tacitus writes the Jewish excursus (5:2-13) in the first person for Roman readers, with the vocabulary of contempt ("superstition", "vilest", "absurd and sordid"). Bloch, reviewed by van der Horst, treats the passage as part of the Greek-Roman ethnographic tradition, shaped for a purpose, and says Tacitus never calls the Jews barbari ("barbarians"). The Annals mention Christ's death (15.44).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:2; Histories of Tacitus 5:5; Histories of Tacitus 5:8

sections.b: Acts has Lysias send Paul to Felix at Caesarea (Acts 23:23-26), where Felix hears him and keeps him two years (Acts 24:22-27). Tacitus names Felix in 5:9 but not the city. Josephus has Titus set out from Caesarea for Jerusalem (Jewish War 5.1.6).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:9; Acts 23:23-26; Acts 24:27

sections.b: Tacitus says Titus added men of the 22nd and 3rd legions brought from Alexandria (5:1); Josephus says he took 2,000 picked men from the Alexandria armies (Jewish War 5.1.6). Alexandria also appears in Titus's earlier work at his father's side there (Jewish War 5.1.1).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 5:1
